# A Small Atlas of Repair

On the first Thursday of every month, the public library in Bellwether stayed open late. Its official calendar called the event a repair clinic, which made it sound cleaner and more authoritative than it was. In practice, six folding tables appeared between the paperback shelves and the windows. People arrived carrying lamps, coats, toys, and appliances in bags whose handles were close to breaking. Extension cords crossed the floor beneath bright yellow tape. Someone made tea. Someone else forgot where the screwdrivers were and found them, inevitably, in the box marked *screwdrivers*.

I began going because I had a broken toaster and no better reason to leave my house. I had moved back to Bellwether that winter, telling people I wanted a change of pace. This was true in the way a weather forecast is true when it says rain is possible. I also had a job I could do from anywhere, a lease I had not renewed, and a sudden uncertainty about what I wanted my days to contain. In Bellwether, I knew the streets well enough to walk them without thinking. I thought that might help.

The toaster was not impressive. Its chrome had dulled, and the lever needed a little encouragement. I had intended to put it on a table, wait while someone declared it finished, and go home with the satisfying knowledge that I had tried. Instead, a woman named Imani asked me to hold a flashlight while she opened the case. She worked slowly and narrated what she was doing, though I was her only audience. There were crumbs everywhere. We tipped them onto a sheet of newspaper. She cleaned a contact, put the cover back, and made a piece of toast. When the bread popped up, both of us looked absurdly pleased.

“You could learn this,” she said.

I told her I doubted it.

“That isn’t what I said.”

So I returned the next month, this time without bringing anything. I held the flashlight again. By spring I knew how to remove a tangled thread from a sewing machine and how to tell when a lamp needed a new plug rather than a new lamp. I also learned to say, “I don’t know,” without feeling that I had disappointed anyone. At the clinic, it was the beginning of nearly every useful conversation.

The tables attracted people who would not otherwise have met. A retired machinist named Cal came with a metal toolbox so heavy that two volunteers had to carry it up the library steps. Nura, who worked at the pharmacy, could mend a seam so neatly that you had to turn a garment inside out to find it. Teenagers came for the volunteer hours their school required and stayed because the work was more interesting than they expected. One boy, Ravi, became the authority on battery compartments after encountering every corroded one in town.

Not everything could be fixed. The clinic had a shelf for objects whose owners wanted to think it over: a blender with a cracked housing, a fan with a motor that smelled burnt, a camera for which no one could find a suitable part. We had a sign that said **PLEASE TAKE YOUR ITEM HOME AT THE END OF THE EVENING**, because before the sign existed, people treated the shelf as a kind of last resting place. I understood the temptation. Leaving an object there meant someone else might decide its fate.

One evening a woman brought in a blue radio wrapped in a dish towel. It was small enough to fit between her hands. The handle had been repaired with string, and the dial’s numbers had nearly worn away.

“My father listened to the games on this,” she said.

Cal opened the back while she watched. The radio had not worked in years. There was dust inside and a loose wire, but Cal would not promise anything. The woman, whose name was Mrs. Alvarez, nodded as though she had expected that answer. Then she sat down beside him and told us how her father used to carry the radio from room to room so he would not miss an inning.

While Cal worked, she described the kitchen of the house where she had grown up. There had been a window over the sink, she said, and through it you could see her father’s tomatoes climbing their stakes. He planted too many every year. By August the family left them on neighbors’ porches, rang the bell, and ran away.

Cal asked her to pass him a small screwdriver. Ravi found fresh batteries in a drawer. For a moment the radio produced only a low rush of static. Then a voice emerged, faint and cheerful, reading the evening weather. Mrs. Alvarez held the radio close, turning it slightly until the signal cleared. She thanked us all, even me, though I had done nothing but listen.

After she left, Imani said that people often brought two things to the clinic: the object they showed us and whatever they could not quite put down on the table. She did not say it solemnly. She was winding a cord around her elbow at the time, trying to make a stubborn coil lie flat.

I thought about Mrs. Alvarez’s radio as I walked home. When my father died, I kept his pocketknife in the top drawer of my desk. It had a nick in the wooden handle where he had dropped it on a stone path, and one blade was too stiff to open comfortably. I had never brought it to the clinic. It did not need repairing. What I wanted was to ask him why he carried it everywhere, although I had seen him use it a hundred times: to cut twine, pare an apple, open a package on the porch. Perhaps I wanted to hear him list those small occasions.

In June, a storm brought down a branch behind the library and knocked out the electricity for half a day. When the lights came back, the clinic’s room reservation had disappeared from the booking system. For one week, we had nowhere to meet. The library staff were apologetic, and Imani said we could simply skip a month. Cal said he already had people asking about a vacuum cleaner and a bicycle. Ravi had promised to look at three game controllers. We moved the tables to the covered pavilion in the park.

That evening was warmer than any we had spent indoors. Moths gathered around the battery lanterns. Children played tag between the picnic benches. We could not test the vacuum cleaner, so its owner stayed to help Nura patch a backpack. A man walking his dog stopped to ask what we were doing and returned half an hour later with a dripping garden hose. We could not repair that either, but we showed him where it had split. He borrowed a pen to write down the size of the connector he needed.

The pavilion night changed the clinic. New people came the following month, carrying things they might previously have thrown away because they had not known whom to ask. A few came carrying nothing and asked whether they could watch. Imani made a second sign: **YOU DO NOT NEED TO KNOW HOW.** She put it at the entrance, where the display of forthcoming library events usually stood.

By autumn, the tables were crowded enough that we began giving out numbered cards. This troubled me. I liked the easy arrivals and the long, wandering conversations. A queue suggested that we ought to work faster, or that someone might be annoyed if we could not reach them. Imani agreed that we needed more volunteers, though she was less sentimental about the old arrangement.

“If people are waiting,” she said, “we should at least get them chairs.”

We asked the library for chairs. Then we asked the town for money for supplies. The town gave us a small grant, and we bought plugs, thread, bicycle cables, glue, storage bins, and a wheeled cart. The grant form required us to estimate how many objects we had kept out of the trash. We counted what we could remember and guessed at the rest, uncomfortable with turning evenings into a number. Still, when the cart arrived, Cal rolled it back and forth across the room like a child with a new bicycle.

As winter approached, we learned the limits of the grant. People needed repairs on days other than the first Thursday of the month. Some could not get to the library in the evening. Some had to decide whether a repair was worth a bus fare, a replacement part, or time away from work. We could help with a zipper or a loose connection; we could not make a washing machine affordable. The longer I volunteered, the less I liked telling people that keeping things in use was simply a matter of caring enough. They cared. They had bills and crowded schedules and no spare lamp to use while theirs sat on our table.

One Thursday a girl arrived with a school backpack whose strap had come away. She stood with her grandmother near the door, looking at the numbered cards. There were eleven people ahead of them. Nura took one look at the bag and invited them to her table. She stitched the strap while the girl described a science project involving bean plants and different kinds of light. When she finished, she showed the girl where to put another row of stitches if the strap began to pull loose again. The girl examined the seam carefully, then asked for a needle so she could try. Nura threaded one for her.

I began to notice how often the person who brought an object went home knowing something about it. Cal drew diagrams on scraps of paper. Ravi made people try the battery cover themselves before he handed back their devices. Imani’s repairs took longer because she liked to explain what she was testing. I was still learning, and sometimes my part was to keep the pieces in order while someone more experienced worked. Even that was useful. A small screw, put back in the right place, can save an hour.

Near the end of the year, I brought in my father’s pocketknife. Its stiff blade had become harder to open, and I was tired of leaving it shut in a drawer. Cal showed me how to clean the joint and work a drop of oil into it. He inspected the nick in the handle and asked whether I wanted to smooth it.

“No,” I said, too quickly.

He handed it back without comment. I opened and closed the blade several times. It moved easily. The nick stayed where it had always been, catching faintly against my thumb.

The following spring, Bellwether received a letter from the company that owned the old mill building by the river. The company wanted to demolish it and build apartments. Some residents hoped the new building would bring customers downtown; others feared the rents would be beyond the reach of people who already lived here. At the clinic, both groups stood in line with broken lamps. We had no special wisdom about the proposal. We disagreed, sometimes sharply, and then borrowed tools from one another. It was awkward to discover that a useful community did not spare us difficult conversations. It gave us a place where we were likely to have them.

At a town meeting, Imani spoke about the library. She wanted longer opening hours and a budget for its maintenance, not merely permission for volunteers to use a room. Cal asked about the bus route, which stopped running before the clinic ended. Nura asked whether the new apartments would include homes her pharmacy coworkers could afford. Their questions went beyond our folding tables. By then we knew how much could be accomplished there, and how much could not.

The mill debate lasted all summer. Some plans changed; many did not. I kept going to the meetings, though I often came home frustrated. On clinic nights I still laid out the tools, checked the tape over the cords, and helped people find a chair. I liked having a task whose edges I could see. I also understood better why Imani stayed after the last visitor had gone, making notes for the library director or drafting another letter to the council.

In September, Mrs. Alvarez returned with the blue radio. I was afraid our repair had failed. Instead, she brought it so Cal could see the little shelf her granddaughter had made for it. She showed us a photograph on her phone: the radio beside a window, a potted plant leaning toward the light. It worked well, she said. Sometimes the signal faded in bad weather, but moving it a few inches usually helped.

Cal looked at the photograph for a long time. Then he asked what kind of wood her granddaughter had used. Mrs. Alvarez did not know. She promised to ask.

That night, after we put the chairs away, I walked home by the river. The mill windows were dark. Across the water, apartment lights came on one by one, showing kitchens, curtains, the brief passage of someone carrying a plate. I had lived in Bellwether for nearly two years. I no longer told people I had moved back for a change of pace. I said I lived here, which was less of an explanation but felt more complete.

At home, I took the pocketknife out of my desk. I opened the blade, cut the string from a parcel, and put the knife on the kitchen table instead of returning it to the drawer. In the morning I would need to break down the box for recycling. I thought my father would have used the knife for that too. Then I made dinner while the box sat by the door, waiting for me to finish what I had started.
